sections.title: Definition of key terms

summary.text: Defines the age groups used in the cryptococcal disease guidelines and terms such as advanced HIV disease, cryptococcal antigen positivity, cryptococcal infection and disease, relapse, sustained clinical response and treatment failure.

sections.extract: Age groups The following definitions for adults, adolescents, children and infants are used in these guidelines for the purpose of implementing recommendations for specific age groups. Countries may have other definitions under national laws. • An adult is a person older than 19 years of age. • An adolescent is a person 10–19 years of age inclusive. • A child is a person one year to younger than 10 years of age. •

sections.title: Executive summary

summary.text: Summarizes the burden of cryptococcal disease in advanced HIV, noting an estimated 181,100 deaths from cryptococcal meningitis in 2014, and explains that these guidelines replace the 2018 edition. It presents the main recommendations on diagnosis, antigen screening, preventive fluconazole and the new preferred induction regimen based on 2021 evidence. The summary also covers consolidation and maintenance treatment, deferred ART, managing raised intracranial pressure and steps for handling relapse.

sections.extract: Cryptococcal disease is one of the most common opportunistic infections among people living with advanced HIV disease and is a major contributor to illness, disability and mortality (1). By far the most common presentation is cryptococcal meningitis, which caused an estimated 223 100 incident cases and 181 100 deaths among people living with HIV in 2014 and accounted for 15% of all the people dying from HIV-related

sections.title: Background

summary.text: Gives the background to cryptococcal disease as an opportunistic infection in advanced HIV, its high mortality especially in low-income countries, and the 2021 trial that prompted the update. It notes that the disease is uncommon in children and mostly presents as meningitis.

sections.extract: Cryptococcal disease is one of the most important opportunistic infections among people living with advanced HIV disease and is a major contributor to illness, disability and mortality (1–5). Clinically significant invasive disease is primarily caused by reactivation of latent infection among immunocompromised individuals, such as people living with HIV, months to years after initial exposure (6). sections.title: Objectives and target audience

summary.text: States that the guidelines aim to give updated recommendations on treating cryptococcal disease in people with HIV and are intended for programme managers, policy-makers, clinicians and people living with HIV.

sections.extract: The objective of these guidelines is to provide updated, evidence-informed recommendations for treating adults, adolescents and children living with HIV who have cryptococcal disease. sections.title: Guiding principles

summary.text: Lists the guiding principles behind the guidelines, such as rapid ART initiation, early diagnosis and antifungal treatment, and deferring ART after a positive antigen screen or confirmed meningitis. It adds that implementation should reflect local epidemiology and context.

sections.title: Diagnosing cryptococcal disease

summary.text: Notes that WHO's 2018 recommendations on diagnosing cryptococcal disease remain unchanged.

sections.extract: The 2018 WHO recommendations for diagnosing cryptococcal disease remain unchanged (16).

sections.title: Background

summary.text: Stresses early diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis and sets out the 2018 recommendation for prompt lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement and rapid antigen testing. It describes diagnostic approaches according to access to lumbar puncture and rapid tests and lists contraindications to lumbar puncture.

sections.extract: Early diagnosis and treatment of cryptococcal meningitis is key to reducing mortality from cryptococcal disease. Health-care professionals should have a low threshold for suspecting cryptococcal meningitis among people with advanced HIV disease. sections.title: Rationale for the recommendations

summary.text: Explains that rapid cryptococcal antigen assays are preferred over India ink because they are more accurate and need less skill, and why lateral-flow assays are favoured. It notes that blood antigen testing does not replace lumbar puncture where feasible and that the adult recommendations are extended to children.

sections.extract: Rapid cryptococcal antigen assay in CSF, serum, plasma or whole blood (depending on access to lumbar puncture) is preferred based on the much higher diagnostic accuracy of these rapid cryptococcal antigen assays versus the India ink test and the fact that these rapid assays depend less on the health-care provider’s skills. sections.title: Preventing and screening for cryptococcal disease

summary.text: Notes that WHO's 2018 recommendations on preventing and screening for cryptococcal disease remain unchanged.

sections.extract: The 2018 WHO recommendations for prevention and screening for cryptococcal disease remain unchanged (16).

sections.title: Background

summary.text: Explains that early ART is the main way to prevent cryptococcal disease and sets out the 2018 recommendations on antigen screening before ART, pre-emptive antifungal therapy and fluconazole prophylaxis where screening is unavailable. It stresses evaluating everyone who screens positive for meningitis.

sections.extract: Early diagnosis and initiation of antiretroviral therapy remains the most important preventive strategy to reduce the incidence of cryptococcal disease among people living with HIV and the associated high mortality.2 Screening for cryptococcal antigenaemia is the optimal approach for guiding resources in a public health approach and is the preferred approach for identifying infection when managing people aged 10

sections.title: Rationale for the recommendations

summary.text: Gives the rationale for screening adults and adolescents with low CD4 counts for cryptococcal antigen before ART and for pre-emptive fluconazole in those who test positive. It covers evaluating antigen-positive people for meningitis and when to stop primary fluconazole prophylaxis, citing trials.

sections.extract: Since 2018, WHO guidelines have recommended that all adults and adolescents living with HIV who have a CD4 cell count <100 cells/mm3 be screened for cryptococcal antigen before ART initiation or reinitiation; cryptococcal antigen screening may also be considered for adults and adolescents living with HIV who have a CD4 cell count <200 cells/mm3. These recommendations were supported by evidence favouring the clinical

sections.title: Recommendations for children

summary.text: Explains that the screening and prophylaxis recommendations are not extended to children because the disease is rare in them, and introduces the new 2022 induction recommendation.

sections.extract: These recommendations apply to adults and adolescents with advanced HIV disease. The decision not to extend these recommendations to children was based on the recognition that cryptococcal disease in this age group is rare, even in countries with high incidence (4,10). These 2022 guidelines provide a new recommendation for the preferred antifungal regimen for the induction phase of treatment.

sections.title: Background

summary.text: Describes the 2018 induction regimens for cryptococcal meningitis based on amphotericin B and flucytosine, along with alternatives when drugs are unavailable, and the extrapolation of evidence to children. It notes that fluconazole monotherapy is not recommended and that WHO met in 2022 to consider a single high-dose liposomal amphotericin B regimen.

sections.extract: The 2018 WHO guidelines recommended seven days of amphotericin B deoxycholate and flucytosine-based therapy (followed by seven days of fluconazole 1200 mg) as the preferred antifungal regimen for the induction phase of treatment of HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis. This was a strong recommendation based on moderate-certainty evidence for adults and low-certainty evidence for children and adolescents (3).

sections.title: Induction therapy

summary.text: Sets out the 2022 recommendation of a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin B with 14 days of flucytosine and fluconazole as preferred induction therapy for cryptococcal meningitis. It lists alternative regimens for when liposomal amphotericin B, any amphotericin or flucytosine is unavailable and stresses the value of flucytosine.

sections.extract: Induction therapy (2022 recommendations) A single high dose (10 mg/kg) of liposomal amphotericin B with 14 days of flucytosine (100 mg/kg per day divided into four doses per day) and fluconazole (1200 mg/daily for adults; 12 mg/kg per day for children and adolescents up to a maximum of 800 mg daily) should be used as the preferred induction regimen for treating people with cryptococcal meningitis. Strong

sections.title: Rationale for the recommendations

summary.text: Reviews the randomized trial in five African countries that compared single high-dose liposomal amphotericin B with the 2018 standard regimen in 844 people with cryptococcal meningitis. It reports that 10-week mortality was 24.8% versus 28.7%, showing non-inferiority, with fewer serious adverse events such as anaemia and kidney toxicity. The section also weighs costs, feasibility, acceptability and equity, noting the reduced burden on health workers.

sections.extract: A systematic review from 2022 identified one randomized trial comparing a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin B, combined with oral flucytosine and fluconazole for 14 days, compared with the preferred induction therapy recommended by WHO in 2018 (38). sections.title: Preventing, monitoring and managing amphotericin B deoxycholate toxicity

summary.text: Sets out good practice principles for preventing, monitoring and managing amphotericin B toxicity, such as hypokalaemia, nephrotoxicity and anaemia. It describes pre-hydration, electrolyte supplementation and laboratory monitoring, and how to weigh continuing deoxycholate treatment when severe anaemia develops.

sections.extract: deoxycholate toxicity Managing toxicity (2022 good practice principles) Infusion-related toxicity and side-effects from amphotericin B therapy are barriers to optimal induction treatment, especially in low- and middle-income countries. • Safe administration of amphotericin B should be given priority and may require referral to a centre with access to the recommended package of preventing, monitoring and managing

sections.title: Drug interactions

summary.text: Describes possible interactions between antifungal drugs and ART, advising kidney monitoring and dose adjustment of tenofovir with amphotericin and haematological monitoring with flucytosine.

sections.extract: Drug interactions in the context of concurrent use of amphotericin, flucytosine and fluconazole alongside ART regimens have not been well documented (45). However, individuals receiving tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF)–based regimens who are receiving amphotericin or recently received amphotericin B preparations should be closely monitored for nephrotoxicity. sections.title: Consolidation and maintenance treatment

summary.text: Restates the unchanged 2018 recommendations for fluconazole doses in the consolidation phase and in maintenance therapy until immune reconstitution.

sections.extract: The 2018 WHO recommendations for consolidation and maintenance treatment for cryptococcal disease remain unchanged (16). Consolidation (2018 recommendation) Recommendation Fluconazole (800 mg daily for adults, 6–12 mg/kg per day for children and adolescents up to a maximum of 800 mg daily) is recommended for the consolidation phase (for eight weeks following the induction phase). Strong recommendation; low-certainty

sections.title: Rationale for the recommendations

summary.text: Explains the evidence behind fluconazole consolidation and maintenance doses and its role in preventing relapse. It also suggests expert-opinion regimens for localized non-meningeal disease, cryptococcomas and disseminated disease.

sections.extract: WHO recommends fluconazole at 800 mg/day for eight weeks following an amphotericin B deoxycholate–based induction regimen; these recommendations were based primarily on expert opinion, considering the limited evidence from two trials that compared itraconazole versus fluconazole at lower doses (48,49). Recent guidelines from the European AIDS Clinical Society recommend 400 mg for eight weeks after a single loading

sections.title: Treatment for pregnant women

summary.text: Advises that amphotericin B may be given in pregnancy when benefits outweigh harm, while flucytosine and fluconazole use should be judged case by case because of possible birth defects.

sections.extract: Amphotericin B therapy can be given to pregnant women with meningeal and non-meningeal disease when the benefits outweigh the harm. Liposomal amphotericin B is considered as a pregnancy category B drug and although animal reproduction studies have failed to demonstrate a risk, an increase in spontaneous abortions was noted at higher doses. sections.title: Adjunctive corticosteroids in treating HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis

summary.text: Restates the 2018 recommendation against routine adjunctive corticosteroids during induction treatment of cryptococcal meningitis, citing trial evidence of more disability and adverse events. It notes that a paediatric advisory group found no reason for a different approach in children.

sections.extract: cryptococcal meningitis Adjunctive corticosteroids (2018 recommendation) Routine use of adjunctive corticosteroid therapy during the induction phase is not recommended in treating adults, adolescents and children who have HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis. Strong recommendation; high-certainty evidence for adults and adolescents and moderate-certainty evidence for children 16 Guidelines for diagnosing,

sections.title: Timing of ART initiation

summary.text: Restates the 2018 recommendation that ART be deferred 4–6 weeks after starting antifungal treatment for cryptococcal meningitis because immediate ART raises mortality.

sections.extract: Timing of ART (2018 recommendations) Immediate ART initiation is not recommended among adults, adolescents and children living with HIV who have cryptococcal meningitis because of the risk of increased mortality and should be deferred 4–6 weeks from the initiation of antifungal treatment. Strong recommendation; low-certainty evidence for adults and very-low-certainty evidence for children and adolescents

sections.title: Rationale for the recommendation

summary.text: Explains the evidence from four trials that early ART after cryptococcal meningitis increases mortality and specifies deferral periods depending on the induction regimen. It also discusses the limited evidence on ART timing for people who are antigen-positive without meningitis.

sections.extract: The optimal timing of ART after cryptococcal meningitis was informed by a systematic review that identified four randomized controlled trials (62). Overall, early ART initiation increased mortality compared with delaying ART initiation (pooled relative risk for mortality at 6–12 months, 1.42, 95% CI 1.02–1.97). Immediately initiating ART is therefore not recommended among people with cryptococcal meningitis because

sections.title: Implementation considerations

summary.text: Advises evaluating people already on ART who develop cryptococcal meningitis for treatment failure and deferring any ART switch by four to six weeks.

sections.extract: ART-experienced people who develop cryptococcal meningitis should be evaluated for potential underlying ART treatment failure, ideally through confirmation by HIV viral load. ART switches should be deferred by four weeks following an amphotericin B–based induction regimen or 4–6 weeks following a fluconazole-based induction regimen.

sections.title: Monitoring and managing people with cryptococcal meningitis
Raised intracranial pressure

summary.text: Explains that raised intracranial pressure affects up to 80% of people with HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis and that lowering it improves survival. It recommends an initial and early repeat lumbar puncture with pressure measurement regardless of symptoms, with therapeutic drainage when pressure is high. Practical notes cover settings without manometers and the volume of fluid that can be removed.

sections.extract: Initial measurement of intracranial pressure and management of raised intracranial pressure are an essential part of cryptococcal meningitis management to prevent death and serious nervous system complications. Raised intracranial pressure is a frequent and potentially life-threatening complication, occurring in up to 80% of people with HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis. sections.title: Cryptococcal immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome

summary.text: Describes cryptococcal immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after starting ART and lists management steps: continue ART, control intracranial pressure, optimize antifungals and consider short-course steroids for life-threatening deterioration.

sections.extract: Paradoxical cryptococcal immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome is associated with high mortality (13). The median time to onset in reported cohort studies is typically 3–12 weeks after initiating ART (67). Raised intracranial pressure is a common feature of cryptococcal immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome and an important contributor to high mortality (68). sections.title: IMPLEMENTATION CONSIDERATIONS

summary.text: Discusses practical issues in implementing the guidelines, including access to rapid antigen assays, laboratory reflex screening and task sharing. It also covers access to essential antifungal medicines, especially flucytosine and liposomal amphotericin B, and adapting the toxicity monitoring package to available resources.

sections.extract: Diagnosis Diagnosis is key to improving mortality from cryptococcal disease, and national programmes need to give priority to reliable access to rapid diagnostic cryptococcal antigen assays, preferably lateral flow assays for use in CSF and serum or plasma. sections.title: RESEARCH NEEDS

summary.text: Lists research needs, such as screening at CD4 counts of 100–200, using blood antigen titres to predict meningitis, managing relapse and integrating screening into advanced HIV care packages.

sections.extract: Further research is needed to assess the value of cryptococcal antigen screening at CD4 cell count thresholds between 100 and 200 cells/mm3, which has been suggested to save costs if carried out in inpatient settings. These guidelines will also be incorporated into the periodic updates of the WHO consolidated guidelines on HIV (75). sections.title: ANNEX 1. Process for developing the guidelines

summary.text: Annex 1 of the WHO cryptococcal disease guidelines outlines how they were developed, from the 2011 rapid advice and 2018 guidelines to a February 2022 Guideline Development Group meeting prompted by new evidence on induction therapy. It explains the use of GRADE to rate evidence certainty and set recommendation strength, and how evidence was summarized and presented. It also describes how declarations of interest from the Guideline Development Group and External Review Group were reviewed and managed.

sections.extract: THE GUIDELINES WHO first published a rapid advice document on the diagnosis, prevention and management of cryptococcal disease in December 2011. In 2018, WHO published guidelines in response to new evidence relating to preventing, screening and treating cryptococcal disease. sections.title: Abstract

summary.text: The abstract of a systematic review on induction therapy for HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis, which found one trial of 844 people comparing a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine and fluconazole with seven days of amphotericin deoxycholate. It reports that the single-dose regimen was non-inferior for 10-week mortality and caused fewer severe adverse events.

sections.extract: Objective: The purpose of this systematic review is to provide updated evidence on the preferred induction therapy for treating people with HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis, considering the most recent evidence available, to inform the need for updates to WHO guidelines. Design: Systematic review. Methods: We searched Medline via PubMed, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library and ClinicalTrials. gov for published or

sections.title: Background

summary.text: Gives the background to the review, noting that cryptococcal meningitis is a leading cause of HIV deaths and that even the 2018 WHO-recommended regimen leaves high mortality and toxicity. It cites a trial in five African countries showing a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin B with two oral antifungals to be as effective, which prompted this update.

sections.extract: Cryptococcal meningitis is a leading cause of HIV-related mortality globally (1). A systematic review and network meta-analysis published in 2018 (2) provided evidence that, in resource-limited settings, one-week intravenous amphotericin B deoxycholate and oral flucytosine induction therapy was superior to other regimens that had been evaluated in clinical trials, and this formed the basis for guidelines published

sections.title: Methods

summary.text: Describes the review methods, including eligibility of randomized trials comparing new induction regimens with WHO-recommended ones in people with a first episode of HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis. It lists outcomes such as 2- and 10-week mortality, fungal clearance and serious laboratory adverse events, and explains the statistical analysis and use of GRADE for certainty.

sections.extract: Eligibility criteria We included randomized controlled trials among people living with HIV with a first episode of cryptococcal meningitis evaluating induction regimens for treating people with cryptococcal meningitis not currently recommended by WHO guidelines. The standard-of-care arm had to include an induction regimen recommended by the WHO guidelines, either one week of amphotericin deoxycholate with

sections.title: Results

summary.text: Reports the study selection, in which one trial of 844 adults in Botswana, Malawi, South Africa, Uganda and Zimbabwe met the criteria, and describes its non-inferiority design. It summarizes the risk of bias and GRADE assessments, rating certainty low for mortality and fungal clearance and moderate for severe adverse events.

sections.extract: Study selection We identified 301 publications through database searches and one additional publication in press arising from an abstract from other sources (Fig. 1). After de-duplication, 276 records were available for reviewing titles and abstracts. Of these 276 records, 267 were excluded since they were not randomized clinical trials involving humans with results available. Nine records were available for full

sections.title: Discussion

summary.text: Discusses the findings, concluding that single high-dose liposomal amphotericin B with flucytosine and fluconazole was non-inferior to standard induction therapy with fewer adverse events. It notes the limitation of relying on one trial and differences between trial and routine settings, and states that WHO issued updated guidelines in March 2022 recommending the regimen, calling for wider access to the drugs.

sections.extract: This updated review identified one study of 844 participants comparing a novel induction strategy for treating people with a first episode of HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis.
